defmodule CleanerCrmWeb.QualityLive.TemplateFormComponent do @moduledoc """ Create/edit a `CleanerCrm.Quality.ChecklistTemplate`: its name, an optional property, and its room-by-room task rows — added and removed with Ecto's `embeds_many` sort/drop params (see `ChecklistTemplate.changeset/2`). On successful save, navigates to the template list directly (rather than notifying the parent), matching `CleanerCrmWeb.ClientLive.FormComponent`'s approach. ## Assigns | Assign | Type | Description | |---------------|--------------------|--------------------------------------------| | id | string | LiveComponent DOM id | | current_scope | `Scope.t()` | caller scope, used for all context calls | | action | `:new \\| :edit` | which mode the form is in | | template | `ChecklistTemplate.t()` | blank (with `items: []`) for `:new`, loaded for `:edit` | | properties | `[{label, id}]` | options for the property picker | ## Dependencies - `CleanerCrm.Quality` """ use CleanerCrmWeb, :live_component alias CleanerCrm.Quality @impl true def render(assigns) do ~H"""
<.header>{form_title(@action)} <.form for={@form} id={"#{@id}-form"} data-test="checklist-template-form" phx-target={@myself} phx-change="validate" phx-submit="save" > <.input field={@form[:name]} type="text" label="Name" data-test="template-name-input" /> <.input field={@form[:property_id]} type="select" label="Property" prompt="Any property" options={@properties} data-test="template-property-select" />

Tasks

<.inputs_for :let={item_form} field={@form[:items]}>
<.input field={item_form[:room]} label="Room" placeholder="Kitchen" /> <.input field={item_form[:task]} label="Task" placeholder="Counters wiped down" /> <.input field={item_form[:required]} type="checkbox" label="Required" />
<.button type="button" name={"#{@form.name}[items_sort][]"} value="new" phx-click={JS.dispatch("change", to: "##{@id}-form")} data-test="add-template-item-button" class="btn-sm" > Add Task
<.button phx-disable-with="Saving..." variant="primary" data-test="save-template-button" > Save Template
""" end @impl true def update(%{template: template} = assigns, socket) do changeset = Quality.change_checklist_template(assigns.current_scope, template) {:ok, socket |> assign(assigns) |> assign(:form, to_form(changeset, as: :template))} end @impl true def handle_event("validate", %{"template" => template_params}, socket) do changeset = socket.assigns.current_scope |> Quality.change_checklist_template(socket.assigns.template, template_params) |> Map.put(:action, :validate) {:noreply, assign(socket, :form, to_form(changeset, as: :template))} end def handle_event("save", %{"template" => template_params}, socket) do save_template(socket, socket.assigns.action, template_params) end defp save_template(socket, :new, params) do case Quality.create_checklist_template(socket.assigns.current_scope, params) do {:ok, _template} -> {:noreply, push_navigate(socket, to: ~p"/quality/templates")} {:error, %Ecto.Changeset{} = changeset} -> {:noreply, assign(socket, :form, to_form(changeset))} end end defp save_template(socket, :edit, params) do case Quality.update_checklist_template( socket.assigns.current_scope, socket.assigns.template, params ) do {:ok, _template} -> {:noreply, push_navigate(socket, to: ~p"/quality/templates")} {:error, %Ecto.Changeset{} = changeset} -> {:noreply, assign(socket, :form, to_form(changeset))} end end defp form_title(:new), do: "New Checklist Template" defp form_title(:edit), do: "Edit Checklist Template" end

2590	  Dynamically adding and removing inputs is supported by rendering named buttons for
2591	  inserts and removals. Like inputs, buttons with name/value pairs are serialized with
2592	  form data on change and submit events. Libraries such as Ecto, or custom param
2593	  filtering can then inspect the parameters and handle the added or removed fields.
2594	  This can be combined with `Ecto.Changeset.cast_assoc/3`'s `:sort_param` and `:drop_param`
2595	  options. For example, imagine a parent with an `:emails` `has_many` or `embeds_many`
2596	  association. To cast the user input from a nested form, one simply needs to configure

Dynamically adding and removing inputs is supported by rendering named buttons for
  inserts and removals. Like inputs, buttons with name/value pairs are serialized with
  form data on change and submit events. Libraries such as Ecto, or custom param
  filtering can then inspect the parameters and handle the added or removed fields.
  This can be combined with `Ecto.Changeset.cast_assoc/3`'s `:sort_param` and `:drop_param`
  options. For example, imagine a parent with an `:emails` `has_many` or `embeds_many`
  association. To cast the user input from a nested form, one simply needs to configure
  the options:

      schema "mailing_lists" do
        field :title, :string

        embeds_many :emails, EmailNotification, on_replace: :delete do
          field :email, :string
          field :name, :string
        end
      end

      def changeset(list, attrs) do
        list
        |> cast(attrs, [:title])
        |> cast_embed(:emails,
          with: &email_changeset/2,
          sort_param: :emails_sort,
          drop_param: :emails_drop
        )
      end

  Here we see the `:sort_param` and `:drop_param` options in action.

  > ### Note {: .info}
  > When using these options, `on_replace: :delete` on the `has_many` and
  > `embeds_many` is required.

  When Ecto sees the specified sort or drop parameter from the form, it will sort
  the children based on the order they appear in the form, add new children it hasn't
  seen, or drop children if the parameter instructs it to do so.

  The markup for such a schema and association would look like this:

  ```heex
  <.inputs_for :let={ef} field={@form[:emails]}>
    <input type="hidden" name="mailing_list[emails_sort][]" value={ef.index} />
    <.input type="text" field={ef[:email]} placeholder="email" />
    <.input type="text" field={ef[:name]} placeholder="name" />
    <button
      type="button"
      name="mailing_list[emails_drop][]"
      value={ef.index}
      phx-click={JS.dispatch("change")}
    >
      <.icon name="hero-x-mark" class="w-6 h-6 relative top-2" />
    </button>
  </.inputs_for>

  <input type="hidden" name="mailing_list[emails_drop][]" />

  <button type="button" name="mailing_list[emails_sort][]" value="new" phx-click={JS.dispatch("change")}>
    add more
  </button>
  ```

  We used `inputs_for` to render inputs for the `:emails` association, which
  contains an email address and name input for each child. Within the nested inputs,
  we render a hidden `mailing_list[emails_sort][]` input, which is set to the index of the
  given child. This tells Ecto's cast operation how to sort existing children, or
  where to insert new children. Next, we render the email and name inputs as usual.
  Then we render a button containing the "delete" text with the name `mailing_list[emails_drop][]`,
  containing the index of the child as its value.

  Like before, this tells Ecto to delete the child at this index when the button is
  clicked. We use `phx-click={JS.dispatch("change")}` on the button to tell LiveView
  to treat this button click as a change event, rather than a submit event on the form,
  which invokes our form's `phx-change` binding.

  Outside the `inputs_for`, we render an empty `mailing_list[emails_drop][]` input,
  to ensure that all children are deleted when saving a form where the user
  dropped all entries. This hidden input is required whenever dropping associations.

  Finally, we also render another button with the sort param name `mailing_list[emails_sort][]`
  and `value="new"` name with accompanied "add more" text. Please note that this button must
  have `type="button"` to prevent it from submitting the form.
  Ecto will treat unknown sort params as new children and build a new child.
  This button is optional and only necessary if you want to dynamically add entries.
  You can optionally add a similar button before the `<.inputs_for>`, in the case you want
  to prepend entries.

  > ### A note on accessing a field's `value` {: .warning}
  >
  > You may be tempted to access `form[:field].value` or attempt to manipulate
  > the form metadata in your templates. However, bear in mind that the `form[:field]`
  > value reflects the most recent changes. For example, an `:integer` field may
  > either contain integer values, but it may also hold a string, if the form has
  > been submitted.
  >
  > This is particularly noticeable when using `inputs_for`. Accessing the `.value`
  > of a nested field may either return a struct, a changeset, or raw parameters
  > sent by the client (when using `drop_param`). This makes the `form[:field].value`
  > impractical for deriving or computing other properties.
  >
  > The correct way to approach this problem is by computing any property either in
  > your LiveViews, by traversing the relevant changesets and data structures, or by
  > moving the logic to the `Ecto.Changeset` itself.
  >
  > As an example, imagine you are building a time tracking application where:
  >
  > - users enter the total work time for a day
  > - individual activities are tracked as embeds
  > - the sum of all activities should match the total time
  > - the form should display the remaining time
  >
  > Instead of trying to calculate the remaining time in your template by
  > doing something like `calculate_remaining(@form)` and accessing
  > `form[:activities].value`, calculate the remaining time based
  > on the changeset in your `handle_event` instead:
  >
  > ```elixir
  > def handle_event("validate", %{"tracked_day" => params}, socket) do
  >   changeset = TrackedDay.changeset(socket.assigns.tracked_day, params)
  >   remaining = calculate_remaining(changeset)
  >   {:noreply, assign(socket, form: to_form(changeset, action: :validate), remaining: remaining)}
  > end
  >
  > # Helper function to calculate remaining time
  > defp calculate_remaining(changeset) do
  >   total = Ecto.Changeset.get_field(changeset, :total)
  >   activities = Ecto.Changeset.get_embed(changeset, :activities)
  >
  >   Enum.reduce(activities, total, fn activity, acc ->
  >     duration =
  >       case activity do
  >         %{valid?: true} = changeset -> Ecto.Changeset.get_field(changeset, :duration)
  >         # if the activity is invalid, we don't include its duration in the calculation
  >         _ -> 0
  >       end
  >
  >     acc - length
  >   end)
  > end
  > ```

defmodule CleanerCrmWeb.QualityLive.TemplatesTest do
  @moduledoc """
  Covers issue 35ce3856: `CleanerCrm.Quality.ChecklistTemplate` had no
  UI to create one and no wiring to a job's checklist, so proof-of-work
  was unreachable through the live product without seeded data. No
  spex/BDD story owns this surface, so it's covered here instead.
  """

  use CleanerCrmTest.ConnCase

  import Phoenix.LiveViewTest

  alias CleanerCrm.Accounts
  alias CleanerCrm.ClientsFixtures
  alias CleanerCrm.Quality
  alias CleanerCrm.SchedulingFixtures
  alias CleanerCrm.Users.Scope

  setup %{conn: conn} do
    user = CleanerCrm.UsersFixtures.user_fixture()
    scope = Scope.for_user(user)
    {:ok, account} = Accounts.create_account(scope, %{name: "Sparkle Co"})
    scope = %{scope | active_account_id: account.id, active_account: account}

    client = ClientsFixtures.client_fixture(scope, %{name: "Riverside Bungalow"})
    property = ClientsFixtures.property_fixture(scope, client, %{service_address: "1 Main St"})

    conn = log_in_user(conn, user)

    %{conn: conn, scope: scope, client: client, property: property}
  end

  test "create_checklist_template supports sort/drop params and a blank property_id",
       %{scope: scope, property: property} do
    {:ok, template} =
      Quality.create_checklist_template(scope, %{
        "name" => "Standard Clean",
        "property_id" => "",
        "items" => %{
          "0" => %{"room" => "Kitchen", "task" => "Wipe counters", "required" => "true"},
          "1" => %{"room" => "Bathroom", "task" => "Sanitize", "required" => "false"}
        }
      })

    assert template.property_id == nil
    assert length(template.items) == 2

    {:ok, updated} =
      Quality.update_checklist_template(scope, template, %{
        "property_id" => property.id,
        "items" => %{
          "0" => %{"room" => "Kitchen", "task" => "Wipe counters", "required" => "true"},
          "1" => %{"room" => "Bathroom", "task" => "Sanitize", "required" => "false"}
        },
        "items_drop" => ["1"]
      })

    assert updated.property_id == property.id
    assert length(updated.items) == 1
    assert hd(updated.items).task == "Wipe counters"
  end

  test "an empty-items create_checklist picks up the job's property template",
       %{scope: scope, client: client, property: property} do
    {:ok, _template} =
      Quality.create_checklist_template(scope, %{
        "name" => "Standard Clean",
        "property_id" => property.id,
        "items" => %{
          "0" => %{"room" => "Kitchen", "task" => "Wipe counters", "required" => "true"},
          "1" => %{"room" => "Bathroom", "task" => "Sanitize", "required" => "false"}
        }
      })

        client_id: client.id,

      })

    {:ok, checklist} = Quality.create_checklist(scope, job, [])

    assert length(checklist.items) == 2
    assert Enum.sort(Enum.map(checklist.items, & &1.task)) == ["Sanitize", "Wipe counters"]

    # client-side "change" event that recalculates the form with a new

    # command found"), so this only checks the button is wired to the
    # right form/param names for a real browser. The row-editing path
    # itself (fill in a room/task, remove a row) is exercised below on
    # a template that already has persisted items, since those rows'
    # inputs genuinely exist in the rendered DOM for `form/3` to target.
    assert has_element?(
             new_live,

           )
